A table is a visualisation too. Column position, alignment, number
formatting, colour, weight: all visual properties, all mappings from data.

## 3a. Tables deserve the same care as plots

Here are the provisional census figures again, as a plain DataFrame. We've
added one column, `growth`: how much each tribe's population grew between
2014 and 2024, as a fraction (0.25 means it grew by 25%).

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: tables_0
#| autorun: true
#| edit: false
import pandas as pd
from great_tables import GT

def load(version):
    p2014 = pd.read_csv(f"data/{version}/census_2014.csv")
    p2024 = pd.read_csv(f"data/{version}/census_2024.csv")
    df = p2014.merge(p2024, on="tribe", suffixes=("_2014", "_2024"))
    df["growth"] = (df.population_2024 / df.population_2014 - 1).round(2)
    return df

provisional = load("bad")
provisional
```

And here is the same data as a finished table, without the growth column:

```{python}
#| echo: false
import pandas as pd
from great_tables import GT, html

def load(version):
    p2014 = pd.read_csv(f"data/{version}/census_2014.csv")
    p2024 = pd.read_csv(f"data/{version}/census_2024.csv")
    df = p2014.merge(p2024, on="tribe", suffixes=("_2014", "_2024"))
    df["growth"] = (df.population_2024 / df.population_2014 - 1).round(2)
    return df

provisional = load("bad")
(
    GT(provisional.drop(columns="growth"), rowname_col="tribe")
    .tab_header(title="Population by tribe", subtitle="Uganda census, 2014 and 2024")
    .tab_spanner(label="Population", columns=["population_2014", "population_2024"])
    .cols_label(population_2014="2014", population_2024="2024")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["population_2014", "population_2024"])
    .tab_source_note(
        "Source: UBOS, National Population and Housing Census 2024, provisional results"
    )
)
```

The finished table is easier to read: it has a title, the numbers have
thousands separators, and the tribe names are set apart from the data.

But it hides the error just as well as the UBOS table did. Better-looking
isn't enough. To reveal the error, a table needs a better **mapping**:
it has to show the right values, in a way the eye can compare. We'll build
up to that.

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: [tables_1, tables_2, tables_3, format_1, format_2, faded, rebuild_1, rebuild_2]
import pandas as pd
from great_tables import GT

def load(version):
    p2014 = pd.read_csv(f"data/{version}/census_2014.csv")
    p2024 = pd.read_csv(f"data/{version}/census_2024.csv")
    df = p2014.merge(p2024, on="tribe", suffixes=("_2014", "_2024"))
    df["growth"] = (df.population_2024 / df.population_2014 - 1).round(2)
    return df

provisional = load("bad")
corrected = load("good")
```

## 3b. Building a table step by step

A great-tables table starts with `GT()`: the data, and which column holds
the row labels. Each method you chain on adds one piece of structure, just
as each `+` adds a layer in plotnine.

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: tables_1
GT(provisional, rowname_col="tribe")
```

`rowname_col="tribe"` moves the tribe names out of the data and into the
**stub**, the column of row labels on the left.

Add a title and subtitle with `tab_header()`:

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: tables_2
(
    GT(provisional, rowname_col="tribe")
    .tab_header(title=___, subtitle=___)
)
```

::: {.hint exercise="tables_2"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

Titles are text, so put them in quotes: `title="Population by tribe"`.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="tables_2"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: tables_2
#| solution: true
(
    GT(provisional, rowname_col="tribe")
    .tab_header(title="Population by tribe", subtitle="Uganda census, 2014 and 2024")
)
```
:::
:::

Now group the two population columns under one heading with
`tab_spanner()`, give the columns short labels with `cols_label()`, and
credit the source with `tab_source_note()`:

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: tables_3
(
    GT(provisional, rowname_col="tribe")
    .tab_header(title="Population by tribe", subtitle="Uganda census, 2014 and 2024")
    .tab_spanner(label="Population", columns=[___, ___])
    .cols_label(population_2014="2014", population_2024="2024", growth="Growth")
    .tab_source_note(
        "Source: UBOS, National Population and Housing Census 2024, provisional results"
    )
)
```

::: {.hint exercise="tables_3"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

`columns` takes a list of column names from the data, in quotes.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="tables_3"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: tables_3
#| solution: true
(
    GT(provisional, rowname_col="tribe")
    .tab_header(title="Population by tribe", subtitle="Uganda census, 2014 and 2024")
    .tab_spanner(label="Population", columns=["population_2014", "population_2024"])
    .cols_label(population_2014="2014", population_2024="2024", growth="Growth")
    .tab_source_note(
        "Source: UBOS, National Population and Housing Census 2024, provisional results"
    )
)
```
:::
:::

A spanner groups *columns* the way `facet_wrap()` groups plots: it shows
which values belong together.

## 3c. Which component?

Match each letter to a part of the table: **header**, **column label**,
**stub**, **body**, **footer**, **spanner**.

```{python}
#| echo: false
def tag(letter):
    return (
        '<span style="display:inline-block;width:16px;height:16px;'
        "line-height:16px;font-size:11px;text-align:center;border-radius:50%;"
        "background:#d7301f;color:white;font-weight:bold;"
        f'vertical-align:super;margin-left:3px">{letter}</span>'
    )

labelled = load("good").head(3)[["tribe", "population_2014", "population_2024"]]
for col in ["population_2014", "population_2024"]:
    labelled[col] = labelled[col].map("{:,}".format)
labelled.loc[1, "tribe"] = labelled.loc[1, "tribe"] + tag("B")
labelled.loc[2, "population_2024"] = tag("D") + labelled.loc[2, "population_2024"]

(
    GT(labelled, rowname_col="tribe")
    .tab_header(title=html("Population by tribe" + tag("C")))
    .tab_spanner(
        label=html("Population" + tag("F")),
        columns=["population_2014", "population_2024"]
    )
    .cols_label(population_2014=html("2014" + tag("A")), population_2024="2024")
    .fmt_markdown(columns=["tribe", "population_2024"])
    .cols_align("right", columns=["population_2014", "population_2024"])
    .tab_source_note(html("Source: UBOS, 2024 census" + tag("E")))
)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

| Letter | Component    | Made with           |
|--------|--------------|---------------------|
| A      | column label | `cols_label()`      |
| B      | stub         | `rowname_col=`      |
| C      | header       | `tab_header()`      |
| D      | body         | the data            |
| E      | footer       | `tab_source_note()` |
| F      | spanner      | `tab_spanner()`     |
:::

## 3d. Formatting as mapping

So far the table shows raw values: `5555412` and `0.27`. The `fmt_*()`
methods map those values to readable text. Format the population columns
as whole numbers and the growth column as a percentage:

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: format_1
(
    GT(provisional, rowname_col="tribe")
    .tab_header(title="Population by tribe", subtitle="Uganda census, 2014 and 2024")
    .tab_spanner(label="Population", columns=["population_2014", "population_2024"])
    .cols_label(population_2014="2014", population_2024="2024", growth="Growth")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["population_2014", "population_2024"])
    .fmt_percent(columns="growth", decimals=0)
)
```

Every number is now readable, and the error is *in* the table: in ten
years, Bagisu shrank by 12% and Acholi by 9%, while every other tribe grew.
Bakiga doubled. But you still have to read each row to find it.

Colour can do that work. `data_color()` maps each value to a background
colour:

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: format_2
(
    GT(provisional, rowname_col="tribe")
    .tab_header(title="Population by tribe", subtitle="Uganda census, 2014 and 2024")
    .tab_spanner(label="Population", columns=["population_2014", "population_2024"])
    .cols_label(population_2014="2014", population_2024="2024", growth="Growth")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["population_2014", "population_2024"])
    .fmt_percent(columns="growth", decimals=0)
    .data_color(
        columns="growth",
        palette=["#d7301f", "white", "#2166ac"],
        domain=[-0.55, 1.05],
    )
)
```

The same table that hid the error now shows it at a glance. Nothing about
the data changed; we chose a different mapping.

::: {.callout-important}
## Why white at 25%?

`palette` lists three colours, and `domain` gives the range of values
they span: red at −55%, blue at +105%, and white halfway, at 25%.

25% is roughly how much the typical tribe grew over the ten years. So
normal growth fades to white, and anything *unusual* stands out, in either
direction: too slow (red) or too fast (blue).

Try centring the scale on zero instead: `domain=[-1.05, 1.05]`. Which
errors can you still see?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Bakiga still stands out in dark blue. But every other growing tribe turns
blue too, and **Bagisu and Acholi fade to a pale pink**: −12% is a small
step from zero on a scale that runs to ±105%. The most impossible numbers
in the table, populations *shrinking*, become the hardest to see.

Where the scale is centred is a design choice, and it decides what the
reader notices. (If a value falls outside `domain`, great-tables colours
it grey, so choose a range that covers your data.)
:::

## 3e. Write the formatting

Fill in the blanks to reproduce this table. Look closely at how the
numbers are written.

```{python}
#| echo: false
(
    GT(provisional, rowname_col="tribe")
    .tab_header(title="Population by tribe", subtitle="Uganda census, 2014 and 2024")
    .tab_spanner(label="Population", columns=["population_2014", "population_2024"])
    .cols_label(population_2014="2014", population_2024="2024", growth="Growth")
    .fmt_number(
        columns=["population_2014", "population_2024"],
        scale_by=1e-6,
        decimals=2,
        pattern="{x}M"
    )
    .fmt_percent(columns="growth", decimals=0)
    .data_color(
        columns="growth",
        palette=["#d7301f", "white", "#2166ac"],
        domain=[-0.55, 1.05]
    )
)
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: faded
(
    GT(provisional, rowname_col="tribe")
    .tab_header(title="Population by tribe", subtitle="Uganda census, 2014 and 2024")
    .tab_spanner(label="Population", columns=["population_2014", "population_2024"])
    .cols_label(population_2014="2014", population_2024="2024", growth="Growth")
    .fmt_number(
        columns=["population_2014", "population_2024"],
        scale_by=___,
        decimals=___,
        pattern="{x}M"
    )
    .fmt_percent(columns="growth", decimals=___)
    .data_color(
        columns=___,
        palette=["#d7301f", "white", "#2166ac"],
        domain=[-0.55, 1.05]
    )
)
```

::: {.hint exercise="faded"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

`scale_by` multiplies each value before it is shown. To show 7,037,404 as
7.04, what do you multiply by? `1e-6` is Python for 0.000001.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="faded"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: faded
#| solution: true
(
    GT(provisional, rowname_col="tribe")
    .tab_header(title="Population by tribe", subtitle="Uganda census, 2014 and 2024")
    .tab_spanner(label="Population", columns=["population_2014", "population_2024"])
    .cols_label(population_2014="2014", population_2024="2024", growth="Growth")
    .fmt_number(
        columns=["population_2014", "population_2024"],
        scale_by=1e-6,
        decimals=2,
        pattern="{x}M"
    )
    .fmt_percent(columns="growth", decimals=0)
    .data_color(
        columns="growth",
        palette=["#d7301f", "white", "#2166ac"],
        domain=[-0.55, 1.05]
    )
)
```
:::
:::

`pattern` wraps the formatted value in text: `{x}` stands for the number.

## 3f. Rebuild the UBOS table

Now build the whole table yourself, from `GT()` up. Aim for a table where
the error would have been obvious *before* publication. Include:

- the tribes as row labels
- a title and subtitle
- a "Population" spanner over the two years
- readable population and growth figures
- colour on the growth column
- the source

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: rebuild_1
(
    GT(provisional, rowname_col="tribe")
    # your code here
)
```

::: {.solution exercise="rebuild_1"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: rebuild_1
#| solution: true
(
    GT(provisional, rowname_col="tribe")
    .tab_header(title="Population by tribe", subtitle="Uganda census, 2014 and 2024")
    .tab_spanner(label="Population", columns=["population_2014", "population_2024"])
    .cols_label(population_2014="2014", population_2024="2024", growth="Growth")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["population_2014", "population_2024"])
    .fmt_percent(columns="growth", decimals=0)
    .data_color(
        columns="growth",
        palette=["#d7301f", "white", "#2166ac"],
        domain=[-0.55, 1.05]
    )
    .tab_source_note(
        "Source: UBOS, National Population and Housing Census 2024, provisional results"
    )
)
```
:::
:::

Now run exactly the same code on the corrected figures. Copy your table
code below, and change `provisional` to `corrected`:

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: rebuild_2
(
    GT(corrected, rowname_col="tribe")
    # your code here
)
```

::: {.callout-important}
## What do you see?

How do the corrected figures look, compared with the provisional ones?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Almost every cell is close to white: every tribe grew by about the usual
amount. The loudest colours are gone.

**Lugbara** stays pink in both tables. Its growth really is low (12% over
the ten years), so that is not an error. Colour shows what is *unusual*, not
what is *wrong*. It tells you where to look, and then you check.
:::

## Plot or table?

In 2f, a plot revealed the error: the change was mapped to the length and
direction of a line. Here a table revealed it: the change was mapped to a
number *and* a colour.

The plot is quicker for spotting a pattern. The table keeps the exact
values, which is what a census report must publish. Both work for the same
reason: they map the growth, not only the raw counts.
